chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from 'Uthman ibn 'Isa from Sama'ah who said:

I asked him about a man who had intercourse with his wife in the month of Ramadan intentionally, so he said: 'Upon him is the freeing of a slave, and feeding sixty poor people, and fasting two consecutive months, and making up for that day, and how can he find like that day?'
So it is possible that the meaning of the 'waw' (and) in the report is the option (to choose one of the expiations) rather than the combination (of all), because it is used for that purpose.
Allah, the Exalted, said: 'So marry of them, those that are lawful to you, two or three or four.'
And he meant two or three or four, and did not mean the combination (of all four at once).

And it is also possible that this ruling is specific to one who had intercourse with his wife in a state where intercourse is forbidden, such as intercourse during menstruation, or in the state of Dhihar before the expiation, for if he did that, the combination of the three expiations becomes obligatory upon him, because he had intercourse in a forbidden manner in the month of Ramadan.
That which indicates this interpretation is what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for intentional intercourse during Ramadan fasting?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this narration from Samaanah, highlighting the juristic debate on whether the three expiations—manumission, feeding sixty poor, and fasting two consecutive months—are cumulative or elective. The text leverages the Quranic usage of 'wa' (and) in marriage verses to argue for an elective reading, while also considering the cumulative application if the act occurred during specific prohibitions like menstruation or Dhihar.
